newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - From the Beehive - The remaking of Peters.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - From the Beehive - The remaking of Peters.

text.p: WELLINGTON, March 14 - The remaking of New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, and to a lesser extent his party, is now almost 100 days old and it has been a rough honeymoon.

When Peters announced his party of protest voters, Maori, Grey Power and disaffected National Party supporters had opted to join the conservative National Party in government in December, it threw NZ First into bed with the party of the very establishment it had made such mileage out of attacking.

The man who had set up in opposition to so many senior business figures; who had got offside with right-wing and left-wing liberals through his coded attacks on immigration; who attacked privilege and vested interest; who was so critical of the offshore investment which flowed from an open economy and of the "monetarist experiment," is now sitting as Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister in the heart of National.
So has he made a change?
Yes, there is agreement to raise spending by $5 billion over three years, and Peters has claimed that as "the difference". Objectively it is doubtful NZ First can claim all the credit.
Postponing $1.1 billion in planned tax cuts means the $950 million extra to be spent in the first year is actually a tighter fiscal position than National proposed.
True, a rise of $2.35 billion in the baseline by 1999/2000, if fulfilled, would be a loosening of the purse strings.

Yet the previous government forecast surpluses of $6 billion by the turn of the century -- clearly unsustainable politically and probably economically unjustified. Any government would have been committed to significant tax cuts or extra spending faced with huge surpluses in the first few years of the next century with debt close to zero.
The inflationary impacts of returning that cash quickly to taxpayers through revenue cuts or spending increases would have not have been relished by the Reserve Bank.
Where Peters party can claim philosophical "victories" is in areas such as Health and Maori Affairs.
So how has Peters performed?

Clearly he is yet to get fully on top of the job, and is uncomfortable in the restrained role Ruth Richardson and Bill Birch made their own. (Late-night altercations in the corridors of power help undermine the carefully nurtured image.)

Those he deals closely with -- Treasury Secretary Murray Horn, Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash and Finance Minister Birch -- reportedly welcome Peters' willingness to build his knowledge in the portfolio. None has said he is on top of it.

So far there have been three important public "events" where the media or other MPs have had a chance to question him at length. At the release of the Treasury briefing papers he asked for time, at the release of the Budget Policy Statement he held a news conference with the media before they saw the document.
At the Finance and Expenditure Committee (FEC) this week he put in a credible display of political acumen but left most questions in the air, while creating later openings.
His claim that being on a low income was not a reason not to save (in defence of compulsory superannuation savings) is just the sort of ammunition the opposition was looking for.
As far as business is concerned, the jury is still out. While it must welcome Peters' conversion to the economic orthodoxy of governments since 1984, he can be equivocal.

Asked about his new-found acceptance of the market in setting the level of the dollar, or his altered position on asset sales or foreign ownership, he frequently points to the need for compromise in the new MMP political environment.

That can leave the impression of a Treasurer implementing policy he accepts in his head but does not support in his heart. That is not to say he can't make the transition. Bill Birch (and most of the 1990-96 National cabinet) made the conversion from protectionists and "think big" proponents to open-market state minimalists.
MPs such as United's Peter Dunne, who as an FEC member was less than impressed with Peters' performance there, think he will thrive only if the economy remains buoyant.

Peters' political problem is that a whole-hearted conversion may undermine the "branding" within the coalition so important to NZ First's chances at the 1999 election, leaving NZ First as an adjunct to National. If the challenges of the first 100 days were difficult, the remaining 30 months of the term present Peters' justifiable reputation for political acumen with its firmest test.
(Note - The opinions expressed are the author's and should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
